transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump acknowledges the Iran war contributed to Republicans' poor performance
during the midterm elections, but says he's not considering replacing Defense Secretary
Pete Hegseth.
NPR's Emily Fang has more on how Trump might handle the war during the new era in Washington.
He seemed to soften his stance a little today.
He said today he could end the war, quote, "any time he wanted."
He said last night on Fox & Friends that he would still strike Iran, though, if Iran,
quote, "does not behave," but also that the two countries could have a diplomatic ending
to this, that they could sign something to end the war.
He has warned that any new major strikes would happen after the midterms, but he's already
said he will not use nuclear weapons.
He told Politico last night he does not need to use nuclear weapons against Iran.
NPR's Emily Fang reporting.
American House Speaker Mike Johnson says he will step aside from congressional leadership
after his party's wipeout in the midterm elections.
Johnson is expected to stay on as a rank-and-file member from Louisiana when the next Congress
convenes in January.
Johnson's decision sets up a fierce internal party battle for his replacement as Republican
leader.
Democrats will control most governorships for the first time in 16 years.
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association, says
it delivers the best map in decades for the 2028 presidential nominee.
Beshear spoke with Kentucky public radio's Sylvia Goodman.
Beshear says the election shows Americans want their governors to focus on everyday
needs and repudiate cruelty.
We will not accept leaders who tell us that our neighbor is the enemy from within and
try to push division between us and people we know simply because they're members of
another party.
He said Americans expect their governors to push back against President Donald Trump,
hinting, for example, to Democrat-led lawsuits over rescinded funding.
Beshear is considered a possible contender for Democratic nominee in 2028 and has hinted
at potential ambitions.
For NPR News, I'm Sylvia Goodman in Louisville, Kentucky.
The United Nations has released a new report finding a "staggering shortfall" of funding
for adapting to the climate crisis.
Here's NPR's Julia Simon.
At the U.N. Climate Conference in Scotland in 2021, world leaders from wealthy countries
committed to increase funding for developing nations most vulnerable to severe storms,
floods, droughts, wildfires, and sea level rise.
Yet, a new U.N. report says wealthy countries are falling short.
Developing countries will need $305 billion a year by 2035 to adapt to climate change
— that's nearly ten times more than what they're getting now.
Next week, countries gather in Turkey for this year's U.N. Climate Conference, where
they will discuss climate finance.
The U.S. federal government will not be in attendance, but some Democratic lawmakers
will.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
The U.S. stocks soared today.
Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm election.
This is NPR News.
A former Manhattan federal prosecutor who oversaw high-profile sex crimes cases against
music mogul Sean Diddy Combs will lead a reopened criminal investigation into gang rape allegations
at Cornell University.
New York's Attorney General Letitia James announced the appointment of Jacqueline Kelly,
who's a Cornell alumna, and is outside counsel for the investigation.
The probe will examine a former student's allegation that several men raped her at a
fraternity party in October 2024.
Today, a NASA space telescope streaked back to Earth like a meteor, and PR's Jeff Brumfield
reports it was a fiery end to a mission that captured some of the biggest and brightest
events in the universe.
It was called SWIFT, and it detected bursts of gamma rays from some of the most powerful
events in the universe.
SWIFT saw black holes shred nearby stars, and the massive explosions from dead stars
colliding together.
When it spotted something, day or night, it sent text alerts to scientists like Kim Page
at the University of Leicester.
It does kind of feel like losing one of the family.
I mean, I've thought about SWIFT every day for 22 years.
NASA has no immediate plans to replace SWIFT, but scientists will continue to study its
data well into the future.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
Among yesterday's ballot measures, Idaho voters have chosen the Winchester Model 1873
as their official state gun, also known as the gun that won the West.
It won with 31 percent of the vote, followed by 25 percent who backed the Winchester Model
1894, and 15 percent who backed the Colt 45.
This is NPR News.
This message comes from Southern New Hampshire University, a nonprofit provider of online
education.
SNHU students are a lot like you.
Parents, professionals with big career plans, and SNHU students do it all while earning
their degrees.
Because with no set class times, low online tuition, and dedicated student support, Southern
New Hampshire University makes going back to school possible.
Get started at snhu.edu/npr.

topics.text: Trump acknowledges Iran war hurt Republicans in midterms but won't replace Hegseth
Trump says he could end Iran war anytime and won't use nuclear weapons
Mike Johnson says he will step aside from House GOP leadership after midterm losses
Democrats win most governorships for first time in 16 years; Beshear touts 2028 map
UN report finds wealthy nations falling short on climate adaptation funding for developing countries
U.S. stocks soar, following typical post-midterm market pattern
Former Manhattan prosecutor to lead reopened Cornell University gang rape investigation
NASA's Swift space telescope re-enters Earth's atmosphere, ending its mission
Idaho voters name the Winchester Model 1873 as official state gun
